profile.intro: Sindrino Matthews is a runner, Burnt Studios athlete, and coach with Must Love Hills Run Crew. From fast road efforts to mountain trails, this is a window into the training, the race days, and the people behind the miles.

philosophy.title: The person before the pace
philosophy.text: Your running belongs in your life. Start with your experience, commitments, and ambitions, and build a rhythm that makes sense for you.

philosophy.title: Consistency over heroics
philosophy.text: Give the everyday work a purpose. Make room for easy running, focused sessions, and time to recover, rather than chasing a breakthrough every day.

philosophy.title: Curiosity, always
philosophy.text: Notice what works. Ask questions. Use your training feedback to keep learning and to shape the next step together.

journal.headline:
A few things
for the road.
journal.intro: Thoughts on training, preparing, and enjoying the process. Practical starting points to take into your next run.

articles.title: Fuel the adventure, not just the race.
articles.excerpt: Make your long run a chance to practise the small things, including what you carry and how you fuel.
paragraphs: Race day is a busy place to try something unfamiliar. Use your training to get comfortable with the food, drink, and carrying system you plan to use.
Start with what you already tolerate. Keep a simple note of the conditions, what you took with you, and how it felt. Bring those observations to a conversation with your coach.

Your needs depend on the person, the effort, the weather, and the event. For an individual nutrition plan, work with a qualified sports dietitian. Keep experimenting away from race day, and give yourself time to find a routine that feels familiar.

articles.title: A calmer mind at the start line.
articles.excerpt: You can’t control every part of race day. A simple routine gives you something familiar to come back to.
paragraphs: Write down the parts of the morning you can organise in advance: your kit, your transport, the start time, and where you need to be.
Pick a small cue you can return to when things get noisy. It might be relaxing your shoulders, looking towards the next marker, or remembering why you signed up.
A goal can give the day direction without defining the whole experience. Leave room to notice the people, the place, and the effort you brought to the line.

articles.title: Let the easy days be easy.
articles.excerpt: Give every run a purpose, including the ones where the purpose is simply to move comfortably.
paragraphs: Before you head out, ask what today’s run is for. If it is an easy day, choose a route and a pace that let it stay that way.
Treat your training notes as a conversation rather than a scorecard. Notice your energy, the conditions, and whether you could talk comfortably.

If your plan and your body are telling different stories, tell your coach. The useful question is what helps you return ready for the next step, rather than what makes today’s numbers look impressive.

articles.title: Less scrambling. More starting.
articles.excerpt: A little preparation helps you give your attention to the experience you came for.
paragraphs: Read the organiser’s current race information. Check registration times, the route, mandatory kit, cut-offs, and any transport arrangements.
Lay out familiar kit and make a short packing list. Check the weather forecast close to the event and adjust within the organiser’s requirements.

Share your expected plans with someone you trust. For a trail event, know the organiser’s emergency process and carry the contact details they specify. Leave yourself enough time to arrive without rushing.

faqs.question: Do I need to be fast to work with a coach?
faqs.answer: Start with your goal and your current experience. Use the contact page to talk about the kind of support you need and whether coaching together is a good fit.

faqs.question: Can we work around my life and schedule?
faqs.answer: Bring your work, family, and training commitments to the first conversation. They are part of understanding what a realistic training rhythm could look like.

faqs.question: How much does coaching cost?
faqs.answer: The proposed options are R450 for a once-off consultation, R950 per month for ongoing coaching, and R1,800 for an eight-week race block. These are draft rates and inclusions; Sindrino will confirm the final arrangement before coaching starts.

faqs.question: What should I include in my enquiry?
faqs.answer: Your running background, the goal or event you have in mind, your available training time, and any questions you would like to discuss.
